lessons.title: Life After the Round: Board, Investor Reporting and Runway Planning

children.text: The money lands, the team celebrates, and the founder wakes up running a different company. There is a board now. Someone expects a monthly update. The plan that existed as a slide is now a commitment, and the bank balance that felt infinite on Friday has a burn rate attached to it. Most of the damage done to startups after a funding round happens in the first 90 days, when spending ratchets up faster than evidence does.

body.text: Raising money does not reduce pressure, it converts it. You have swapped the risk of running out of cash for the obligation to turn that cash into proof, on a clock, in front of people who will decide whether to fund you again.

body.title: What to do with the quarter after closing

events.title: Close the loop on compliance
events.description: Complete allotment, filings, certificates and registers. Save the whole pack in the data room while it is fresh, because the next round's diligence will ask for it.

events.title: Convert the plan into a budget
events.description: Turn the use of funds from the deck into a month-by-month hiring and spending plan, with the milestones each rupee is meant to buy.

events.title: Set the reporting rhythm
events.description: Agree the board calendar, the update format and the metrics definitions now, while everyone is friendly and nobody is under pressure.

events.title: Hire the roles the round was raised for
events.description: In the order the plan says, not in the order candidates appear. Every hire raises burn permanently and is far harder to reverse than to make.

events.title: First real board meeting
events.description: Not a celebration. A pre-read, a dashboard, two or three genuine decisions and minuted outcomes.

body.text: The most expensive mistake after a round is hiring ahead of evidence. Salaries are the one cost that never falls on its own. A team of 12 that becomes 30 in four months has tripled the monthly burn before a single new hire has proved anything, and the only way back is layoffs, which cost morale, reputation and momentum all at once.

body.title: What burn does the plan allow?
body.prompt: A startup raises ₹24 crore and tells its investors the round funds 24 months of operations. Ignoring any revenue, what is the maximum average net burn per month, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹24 crore ÷ 24 months = ₹1 crore a month on average. If burn drifts to ₹1.6 crore, the same money lasts 15 months, and the company is back in the market before the milestones it promised are anywhere close. Set this ceiling on day one and review it monthly, because burn rises quietly through many small decisions rather than one big one.

children.text: The Board: From Formality to Useful

Indian companies must hold board meetings at a prescribed minimum frequency through the year, with limits on the gap between them, so the meetings will happen regardless. The question is whether they are worth the day they consume. The difference between a useful board and an expensive ritual is almost entirely about preparation.

columns.label: Performance theatre
points: Deck circulated the night before, or in the room
Forty slides of what everyone already knows
Founder spends the meeting defending the past quarter
Bad news arrives softened, or not at all
No decisions, vague minutes, and the same discussion next quarter

columns.label: A board that earns its day
points: Pre-read sent 3 to 5 days in advance, and actually read
One dashboard page, then straight to the hard questions
Founder brings the two problems they cannot solve alone
Bad news arrives first, with options attached
Clear decisions, named owners, minuted and reviewed next time

body.title: A one-page board pre-read that works

children.text: Send this three to five days before the meeting, so the discussion starts where the document ends.
revenue, growth, retention, cash, net burn, runway and headcount, each shown against plan and against last quarter. Same definitions every time.
three things that went well, three that did not, in plain language and without spin.
two or three real choices, each with the options, your recommendation and what you need from the board.
specific introductions, candidates or customers you want help with, named where possible.
Keep the statutory business, approvals and minutes as a separate agenda item handled by the company secretary, so governance does not crowd out the discussion you actually need.

body.caption: Who hears what, and how often

cells: Pipeline, shipped work, blockers, the one number that matters this week
Metrics, cash and runway, wins, lowlights, specific asks
Pre-read, dashboard against plan, decisions, budget review, statutory items
Audited accounts, next year's budget, ESOP pool review, statutory filings
Anything material: a lost anchor customer, a co-founder leaving, a regulatory notice, a security incident

body.label: Why the monthly update matters more than it looks
body.value: It is next round's evidence, written in advance
body.context: Twelve honest monthly updates give an investor a record of a founder who forecasts accurately and says hard things early. That track record does more for your Series A than any pitch, and it is the cheapest asset you can build.

body.title: The monthly investor update, in five blocks
steps: Metrics: revenue, growth, retention and the two or three numbers specific to your model, always defined the same way.
Cash: closing balance, net burn and runway in months, stated plainly.
Wins: what genuinely moved, with the name of the customer or hire where you can share it.
Lowlights: what went wrong and what you are doing about it. This section is why people trust the rest.
Asks: three specific requests, such as an introduction to a named company, a candidate profile, or advice on a decision.
Send it by a fixed date every month, even in bad months, especially in bad months.

body.text: Investors are not scored on how calm your updates are. A founder who writes "churn rose to 4.1% this month, here are the three reasons and what we are changing" gets help. A founder who reports only wins for five months and then asks for a bridge round gets a very different conversation. Surprises are what damage trust, not problems.

stats.label: Track monthly
stats.context: The three numbers a founder should know without opening a file

stats.label: Plan in scenarios
stats.context: Know in advance which costs get cut at which trigger point

stats.label: Hire against milestones
stats.context: Each role tied to the evidence it is meant to produce

stats.label: Protect the reserve
stats.context: The cash that lets you negotiate the next round instead of accepting it

children.text: The single most useful discipline is the trigger plan: decide today, in writing, what you will do if growth is 30% below plan at month 9. Which hires pause, which experiments stop, which contracts do not get renewed. Founders who write this down act early and calmly. Founders who do not tend to act four months late, when the options are worse.

body.title: The bad quarter
body.question: Six months after a seed round, revenue growth has stalled and burn is 25% above plan. What should the founder do first?
options: Wait for the quarterly board meeting so there is more data to explain the dip
Tell the board and lead investor now, with the cause, the revised runway and two options for the response
Cut marketing spend quietly and mention it if anyone asks
Start approaching new investors for a bridge round before the current ones find out
body.explanation: Early, specific disclosure with options attached is what keeps investors useful. Waiting for the scheduled meeting wastes a month of runway, quiet cuts look like concealment once discovered, and raising a bridge behind your existing investors' backs damages the relationship you most need when things are difficult.

body.title: Eight months in, and the maths has moved
body.scenario: Kabir raised ₹18 crore nine months ago, planning 24 months of runway at ₹75 lakh a month. Headcount went from 14 to 41. Net burn is now ₹1.45 crore a month and ₹8.6 crore of cash is left. Revenue has grown from ₹40 lakh to ₹62 lakh a month, well behind the plan of ₹1.1 crore. His investors have seen four updates, all positive.
body.prompt: Work out the real position and set out what Kabir should do over the next 30 days.
body.modelAnswer:
First, the arithmetic. At ₹1.45 crore a month, ₹8.6 crore is under 6 months of runway, not the 15 months the original plan implied. He is already inside the window where he should be raising, and his growth does not yet support a Series A.
Week 1: tell the truth. A written update to the board and lead investor with the revised runway, the burn bridge showing how ₹75 lakh became ₹1.45 crore, and the gap between planned and actual revenue. Four positive updates in a row have made this conversation harder than it needed to be, which is itself a lesson.
Week 1 to 2: rebuild the plan in three scenarios. Base, slow and bad, each with a burn ceiling and a named list of what gets cut at which trigger. Identify the spending that is not producing evidence, which at 41 people usually includes roles hired ahead of demand.
Week 2 to 3: decide on the cut, and make it once. A reduction taken fully and early preserves more runway and more trust than three rounds of small trims. Target a burn that gives at least 12 months, which from ₹8.6 crore means roughly ₹70 lakh a month.
Week 3 to 4: agree the next milestone with the board. Either reach the metrics that justify a Series A, or reach profitability at a smaller scale. Then ask the investors directly whether they will support a bridge, and on what evidence, so it is a planned conversation and not an emergency one.
The underlying error was not the hiring, it was reporting only good news while burn nearly doubled. Monthly updates exist precisely so this conversation happens at month three, not month nine.

children.text: A funding round reshapes working life well beyond the founders. HR and talent teams suddenly have a headcount plan tied to milestones rather than to gut feel, and ESOP grants to administer properly. Finance teams inherit monthly reporting discipline, a board pack and an audit that will be examined. Managers find that budgets now come with questions about what evidence the spending produces. Employees hold options whose value depends on decisions made in a boardroom they never enter. Understanding the rhythm of a funded company, and being able to read a runway number, is genuinely useful whether or not you ever raise a rupee yourself.

body.title: The number to protect
body.textWithBlank: The cash reserve that lets a founder negotiate the next round instead of accepting whatever is offered is measured in months of ___.
body.explanation: Runway is leverage. A founder with two months of cash takes the terms on the table. A founder with nine months can say no, which is usually what makes the terms improve.

cards.definition: The document sent several days before a board meeting, so the meeting starts with decisions rather than catch-up.
A short standing update covering metrics, cash, wins, lowlights and specific asks, sent on a fixed date.
The deliberately honest section of an update. It is what makes the rest of the update credible.
A written decision, made in advance, about what gets cut if performance falls below defined thresholds.
The maximum average monthly burn the round's runway allows, set on day one and reviewed monthly.
Additional funding between priced rounds, usually from existing investors, to extend runway to a milestone.

points: Raising money converts pressure rather than removing it: cash risk becomes an obligation to produce proof on a clock.
Most post-round damage happens in the first 90 days, when hiring outruns evidence and burn rises permanently.
Set a burn ceiling on day one. ₹24 crore for 24 months means ₹1 crore a month, and drift to ₹1.6 crore costs you nine months.
Board meetings are worth the day only if there is a pre-read, a consistent dashboard, real decisions and minuted owners.
Send a monthly update to every investor, with lowlights and specific asks. Twelve honest updates are your next round's strongest evidence.
Report material bad news immediately, with options attached. Surprises damage trust far more than problems do.
Write the trigger plan before you need it, and protect a reserve of several months so you can negotiate the next round rather than accept it.
A round changes working life for HR, finance, managers and ESOP-holding employees, not just for the founders.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Board meeting frequency and governance requirements under Indian company law vary by company type and change over time, so confirm the requirements applicable to your company with a qualified company secretary. Kabir's company and all figures are illustrative.
